i2.en: A small site for the mechanical parts of doctoral writing

i3.en: I built this site while writing my own doctorate, because I was losing hours to reference formatting that should have taken minutes. These are the tools I wished existed: small, transparent, and honest about what they cannot do.

i5.en: Reference styles, dissertation templates and reference managers each implement a slightly different version of the same rules. The result is that doctoral candidates spend hours on punctuation while supervisors spend hours marking it. The problem is not intellectual difficulty; it is that the rules are numerous, mostly mechanical, and badly served by tools that hide what they did.

i6.en: This site takes the opposite approach. Each tool is small, does one job, shows its output in both formatted and plain text, and explains the rule being applied on the same page. Where a rule cannot be applied reliably — automatic sentence-case conversion is the clearest example — the tool declines to guess and tells you what to check instead.

i8.en: If one entry in your list is still wrong and you cannot see why, email it to me. I will check it against APA 7 and tell you exactly what to change — free, no sign-up, no mailing list. I do this because a broken citation is usually a symptom of a rule nobody explained properly, and fixing it with you tells me which rule needs a better tool or a clearer guide.

i10.en: One entry, pasted into an email. Please do not send drafts, chapters or participant data. If it helps, I will also send you the submission checklist I use on my own manuscript.

i14.en: The tools are plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework, no build step, no third-party runtime library and no network calls. They run entirely in your browser. i15.en: This is a deliberate design decision, not just a privacy feature. A tool with no dependencies has no licence obligations to audit, no supply-chain updates to track, and no risk of a CDN going down the night before a submission deadline.

i2.en: APA 6 to APA 7: what actually changed

i3.en: If your reference manager still thinks it is 2009, this is the list of things that will be wrong. Most of them are mechanical, all of them are findable, and none of them require re-reading the manual.

i4.en: Why a migration guide is worth more than a style summary

i5.en: A thesis written under APA 6 does not become APA 7 by changing the heading. The differences are small, numerous and invisible unless you know to look for them. Worse, reference managers keep the style they were given when the database record was created, so a 2016 export can silently carry 2009 punctuation into a 2026 submission. The reliable approach is to migrate once, deliberately, and then check with a tool that flags the old patterns.

i6.en: Below is every change that affects the average dissertation or journal manuscript, grouped by where you will meet it. Each item gives the old form and the new one.

i8.en: APA 7 removed the city of publication from book and report references. This is the most visible change in a reference list and the easiest to fix in bulk.

i9.en: Keep the publisher name exactly as it appears on the copyright page, but drop "New York:", "London:" and any state abbreviation. Do not replace the location with a URL unless you are citing a work you accessed online and your institution asks for the link.

i11.en: APA 6 prefaced web addresses with Retrieved from as a matter of course. APA 7 uses the bare URL. The exception is narrow: when a page is designed to change over time and you need to show when you saw it, give a retrieval date.
i11.html: APA 6 prefaced web addresses with Retrieved from as a matter of course. APA 7 uses the bare URL. The exception is narrow: when a page is designed to change over time and you need to show when you saw it, give a retrieval date.

i12.en: A journal article from a database is not a dynamic source. If it has no DOI, end the entry at the page range and add nothing. The automatic "Retrieved from" in older BibTeX records is one of the highest-yield search-and-replace operations in a migration.

i16.en: 4. Three or more authors: et al. from the start

i17.en: This is the change people notice first in the text. APA 6 asked you to list up to five authors on first citation and switch to et al. from the sixth. APA 7 uses et al. from the first citation whenever a work has three or more authors.

i18.en: The reference list moved in the opposite direction: it now enumerates up to twenty authors in full, and only with twenty-one or more do you list the first nineteen, an ellipsis, and the final author. A six-author paper under APA 7 has a short in-text citation and a long reference entry. That asymmetry is intentional and catches people who assume the two lists should mirror each other.

i20.en: APA 7 added square-bracketed labels after the title when the source type is not obvious from the entry. Dissertations, theses, datasets, software, maps and conference presentations are the common cases.

i21.en: The bracketed element is not italicised and sits inside the title's sentence, followed by a period. The repository or database name comes after the bracket, not before it. For the full set of dissertation patterns, see citing dissertations and theses in APA 7.

i24.en: The practical migration task is to check every web entry for three things: a site name that is currently missing, a date that is currently guessed, and a full-width punctuation mark that came from a Chinese-language source.

i26.en: APA 7 changed the layout of table and figure components. Both now use a bold number on its own line, followed by an italic title on the next line. Notes come below the body in a specific order: general note, specific note, probability note. Statistical and mathematical copy follows a tighter set of rules too, including no leading zero before values that cannot exceed one.

i2.en: Citing a dissertation or thesis in APA 7

i3.en: Dissertation entries are where the manual and the institutional template most often disagree. Here is how to build one, what the square brackets actually do, and the six patterns that cover almost every case.

i4.en: Start with one question: published or not?

i5.en: APA 7 treats a dissertation that has been made available in a database or institutional repository differently from one that exists only as a bound copy on a shelf. The distinction decides whether your entry ends with a repository name or with an availability phrase.

i6.en: A published dissertation means it is retrievable by a reader — through ProQuest, an institutional repository, a library catalogue with a stable link, or the university's own archive. It does not mean it went to a commercial press. An unpublished dissertation is one a reader cannot obtain; you cite it with an availability statement and no URL.

It does not mean it went to a commercial press. An unpublished dissertation is one a reader cannot obtain; you cite it with an availability statement and no URL.

i8.en: Every dissertation reference is still author, date, title, source. What changes is the source element and the bracketed label attached to the title.

i9.en: Three rules govern this line. First, the title is italicised but the bracketed description is not. Second, the bracket sits immediately after the title, before the period. Third, the institution goes inside the brackets, not after them — a detail carried over from APA 6 that still appears in a lot of thesis templates.

i11.en: The label identifies the type of work when the title alone would not. For a doctorate write [Doctoral dissertation, Institution Name]. For a master's write [Master's thesis, Institution Name]. For a professional doctorate use the degree actually awarded: [Doctor of Business Administration dissertation, Institution Name] is more accurate than the generic form, and accuracy beats brevity in a viva.

i13.en: Six templates that cover nearly everything

i14.en: 1. Published dissertation in a commercial database

i15.en: The database name is not italicised. Include the publication number only if the database supplies one and your institution asks for it; it is useful for retrieval but not required by APA 7.

i16.en: 2. Published dissertation in an institutional repository

i17.en: Here the repository name is the source element, followed by the stable link. If the repository itself is the institution, name it once in the brackets and give the link without repeating the name.

i18.en: 3. Unpublished dissertation, reader cannot retrieve it

i19.en: No repository, no URL, and no database. The bracket carries both the status and the institution. Use this only when it is true — if the thesis is in a catalogue with a record, it is retrievable and belongs under pattern 1 or 2.

i21.en: Identical structure, with Master's thesis in the bracket. The apostrophe matters: Master's, not Masters.

i23.en: Only Chen appears in your reference list. Use this when the original is genuinely inaccessible, then try to obtain it — a chain of dissertations citing dissertations is a common examination question.

i25.en: You cite your own work exactly as you would anyone else's, in third person, with your full name. Do not write "my dissertation" in the text of a paper derived from it. If the dissertation is still in progress and not yet deposited, cite the individual papers already published from it rather than the thesis itself.

i27.en: The label should reflect the qualification. If the award is a DBA, EdD or DProf, name it. This matters more than it looks: examiners in professional doctorates often check whether the candidate understands the distinction between a research doctorate and a professional one, and the reference entry is one of the places that shows it.

i2.en: APA 7 in-text citations, decided in one page

i3.en: The reference list gets all the attention. In-text citations are where most supervisor comments actually land. Here is every pattern you will need, with the two decisions that cause almost all the errors.

i4.en: The two forms: parenthetical and narrative

i5.en: Every in-text citation is either parenthetical — author and year inside brackets at the end of the sentence — or narrative, where the author is part of your sentence and only the year sits in brackets. The meaning is identical. The choice is about what you want the reader to notice.
i5.html: Every in-text citation is either parenthetical — author and year inside brackets at the end of the sentence — or narrative, where the author is part of your sentence and only the year sits in brackets. The meaning is identical. The choice is about what you want the reader to notice.

i6.en: Use the narrative form when the researcher is the point of the sentence; use the parenthetical form when the claim is the point. In a literature review, alternating the two keeps the prose from becoming a list of names at the end of every sentence. What you must not do is mix the punctuation: narrative citations take a comma before the year only when the author element ends in a possessive or a suffix; otherwise the year follows the names directly.

i7.en: One rule that surprises people: in the narrative form, two authors are joined with "and", not the ampersand. In the parenthetical form they are joined with &. That is the only place in APA 7 where the connector changes.

i8.en: Author count: the entire decision table

i30.en: The et al. rule changed in APA 7

i31.en: This is the single most common carry-over error from APA 6. Under the sixth edition you listed every author up to five, then used et al. from the sixth. APA 7 uses et al. from the first citation whenever there are three or more authors. A 20-author paper is cited as (Smith et al., 2024) on first mention, even though the reference list below enumerates all twenty.

APA 7 uses et al. from the first citation whenever there are three or more authors. A 20-author paper is cited as (Smith et al., 2024) on first mention, even though the reference list below enumerates all twenty.

i32.en: Two details that get marked: et al. has a period after al. but not after et; and there is a comma between the author element and the year, so (Smith et al., 2024) — not (Smith et al. 2024). In the narrative form the same rule applies: Smith et al. (2024) found...

i33.en: The reference list behaves differently. There, et al. never appears. Twenty or fewer authors are all named; with 21 or more you list the first nineteen, an ellipsis, then the final author. If your in-text citation says et al. and your reference entry also says et al., one of them is wrong.

If your in-text citation says et al. and your reference entry also says et al., one of them is wrong.

i35.en: Organisations are authors in their own right. Spell the name in full on first use, and introduce a short form in square brackets if you intend to use it later. After that first citation, the short form alone is enough.

i36.en: Do not invent an abbreviation that could be confused with a person's surname, and do not abbreviate a group name that is already short. "The World Bank" is fine as written; turning it into (WB, 2024) makes the reader work harder for no gain. If two of your sources share the same abbreviation, spell both out every time.

i38.en: When one author has two works from the same year, append lowercase letters in alphabetical order of the reference titles: 2020a, 2020b. The letters are assigned by title, not by publication month or by the order you read them. Once assigned, they must match in the text and in the reference list, and the suffixes attach to the year inside the same parentheses.

The letters are assigned by title, not by publication month or by the order you read them. Once assigned, they must match in the text and in the reference list, and the suffixes attach to the year inside the same parentheses.

i39.en: Do not add a letter to a single work just because another year is close. 2023 and 2024 need no letter. The letters only disambiguate an exact year collision for the same author or same author team.

i40.en: No author, no date, in press

i41.en: If a work genuinely has no author, move the title into the author position. i2.en: A reproducible literature review workflow for doctoral students

i3.en: A literature review is judged on the argument, but it is defended on the audit trail. This seven-stage workflow is designed so that any search, exclusion or coding decision can be reconstructed months later, when a supervisor or examiner asks why a particular study is missing.

i4.en: Why reproducibility matters more than volume

i5.en: Doctoral candidates often respond to uncertainty by reading more. Reading more is rarely the problem. The failure mode is losing the ability to explain how the corpus was assembled: which database, which exact string, which date, which inclusion rule, and why the 2008 paper was excluded while the 2009 paper was kept. In a DBA or other professional doctorate, where the review usually supports an applied research question, an examiner is entitled to ask whether the search was systematic enough to support the claims being made. A clean, boring audit trail answers that question better than an impressive reading list.

i6.en: The workflow below borrows the discipline of a systematic review without requiring you to register a protocol or produce a PRISMA diagram, unless your institution asks for one. It works in a spreadsheet plus a reference manager, with no specialist software.

i7.en: Stage 1: write the question before the search string

i8.en: Write one sentence stating the construct, the population or context, and the relationship of interest. Then list the synonyms for each concept. Search strings are built from those synonym lists, not from intuition on the day. For a study of dynamic capabilities and financial performance in Chinese firms, the concept buckets might be dynamic capabilities / absorptive capacity / organisational agility, financial performance / firm performance / ROA / Tobin's Q, and China / Chinese firms / emerging markets.

i9.en: Save the question and the synonym list in a file called review-protocol.md inside your project folder. Date it. That single file is what turns a pile of PDFs into a defensible method.

i10.en: Stage 2: log every search exactly as run

i11.en: Create a search log with one row per query: date, database, the full string copied verbatim, field restrictions, date limits, language limits, and the number of hits. Copy-paste the string; do not paraphrase it. Databases change their syntax and their coverage, and "a search of Web of Science" is not a method — "TITLE-ABS-KEY(...) AND ... run on 2026-03-14, restricted to 2010-2026, 1,284 records" is.

i26.en: Stage 4: screen in two passes with a written rule

i27.en: First pass: title and abstract against inclusion and exclusion criteria written before you start. Second pass: full text. Keep a screening log with one row per record and a reason code for every exclusion. i29.en: Stage 5: build a synthesis matrix, not an annotated bibliography

i30.en: An annotated bibliography is a list of summaries arranged by author. A synthesis matrix is a table arranged by concept, which is what a literature review chapter actually needs. Columns typically include: citation, theoretical lens, construct definition, sample and context, method, key finding, measured outcome, limitations, and how it relates to your research question. One row per study; one column per concept you will write about.

i31.en: The payoff is structural. When every study's definition of the central construct sits in a single column, the inconsistencies in the literature become visible as a pattern rather than as twelve disconnected paragraphs. That pattern is usually the contribution of your review: not "researchers have studied X", but "researchers mean three different things by X, and the empirical results divide along those definitions".

i2.en: Why your reference manager keeps exporting Title Case

i3.en: You change the style to APA 7, export again, and every article title is still Capitalised Like This. The problem is not the style file. It is the data underneath it — and the fix is not the one most people try.

i4.en: The database stored capitals, not words

i5.en: Most bibliographic records arrive from publisher databases with titles already capitalised. Web of Science, Scopus, Crossref and the publisher's own site typically supply the title in title case, because that is how journal tables of contents are typeset. Your reference manager imports that string and stores it as-is. The output style then decides what to do with it.

i6.en: Here is the crucial distinction: an APA 7 style file changes punctuation, order and italics. It does not reliably change the case of the letters you stored. Some styles apply a case transformation at export; many do not, and those that do are inconsistent across reference types. So the same library can export one article title in sentence case and the next in Title Case, depending on where each record came from.

i7.en: This is why changing the style again rarely helps. The style is behaving correctly with the data it was given. The capitals are in the record.

A case converter is a simple algorithm: lowercase everything except the first word and the word after a colon. It has no idea what a proper noun or a named construct is. The damage is silent, because the result still looks plausible.

i40.en: What the builder does, and what it deliberately refuses to do

i41.en: APA 7 reference entries follow a four-element structure: author, date, title, and source. The builder assembles those four elements in the right order for the source type you select, because the fourth element is the one that changes most: a journal article needs an italic journal title and volume, a book needs a publisher, a chapter needs an "In" clause with editors and page range, and a dissertation needs a bracketed description plus its repository.

i43.en: Names entered as "Smith, John A." are reduced to "Smith, J. A."; names entered as "John A. Smith" are inverted first. Hyphenated given names such as "Jean-Luc" become "J.-L." For a compound surname or a suffix such as "Jr.", use the Surname, Given form so the tool does not split the surname. The tool does not attempt to detect nobility particles, particles such as "van der", or organisation names with internal commas — enter those carefully and proofread the result.

i44.en: The number of authors changes the punctuation. One author ends with a period. Two authors are joined with , & . Three to twenty authors use a serial comma before the ampersand. With twenty-one or more, APA 7 lists the first nineteen, inserts an ellipsis, and then gives the final author with no ampersand; the builder implements that rule and tells you when it fires.

i46.en: Reference titles take sentence case: capitalise the first word, the first word after a colon, and proper nouns. Converting Title Case automatically sounds easy but fails on acronyms, chemical names, proper nouns and discipline-specific capitalisation (for example "Dynamic Capabilities" may be a named theoretical construct in your field). The builder therefore preserves the title exactly as you type it and raises a warning when it detects three or more capitalised words that look like Title Case or ALL CAPS. Export tools and bibliographic databases commonly deliver Title Case; this is the single most common thing to fix after an import.

i48.en: For journal articles, the journal name and the volume number are italicised; the issue number in parentheses is not. For books and dissertations the title is italicised, and for web pages the site name is italicised unless it is identical to the author. A DOI is normalised to https://doi.org/... whether you paste the bare identifier, a doi: prefix, a dx.doi.org link or the final URL. No terminal period is added after a DOI or URL because it tends to be copied as part of the link.
